analysis.one_liner: Lets insurers pick one state's rules and sell lighter-regulated individual health plans in every other state.
analysis.headline: The bill had no cosponsors and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change which state's rules apply when an insurer sells individual health coverage across state lines. Each insurer would pick one 'primary state,' and that state's insurance laws would govern the policy everywhere it is sold. The insurer would be exempt from most of the other state's insurance laws, including its consumer protections, benefit requirements, and rules on premium changes, though it would still have to follow a short list of protections like fraud and claims-settlement rules and an outside appeals process. The bill required a government study of its effects but never advanced past its first committee stop.
analysis.who_benefits: Health insurers, which could choose a state with lighter rules and sell plans nationwide under that state's laws while avoiding the consumer protections of every other state. Some individual buyers, especially healthy people who need little care, could find lower-priced plans, though the bill's own required notice tells buyers those plans 'may be less expensive than others because it is not subject to all of the insurance laws' of their state, including some required benefits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Health insurers selling across state lines

how_it_helps.text: Would let a health insurer designate one 'primary state' whose insurance laws govern its individual coverage in all other states, and would exempt the insurer from any other state's laws that prohibit or regulate its operation there.
Would give the primary state sole authority to enforce its insurance laws in every state where the plan is sold, leaving other states unable to apply their own rules to the plan.

Kept a narrow set of protections: buyers would get a bold-face notice that the plan is not subject to all of their state's consumer protections or required benefits, coverage could not be reclassified or repriced based on health status at renewal, certain protected individuals must be offered coverage, and plans sold across state lines must include an independent appeals process for denied claims.

analysis.who_pays: Buyers of the out-of-state plans, who would lose the benefit mandates, consumer protections, and restrictions on premium changes of the state where they live. State governments and their insurance regulators would lose most of their authority over plans sold to their own residents. The bill directs a five-year government study of whether the change increases the uninsured rate, raises costs for people with pre-existing conditions, and strips benefits from policies — concerns the bill itself acknowledges as open questions.

drawbacks.text: Other states could not apply their own consumer protections, required benefits, or rate-change restrictions to plans sold to their residents; the bill's required notice tells buyers the policy 'is not subject to all of the consumer protection laws or restrictions on rate changes of the State.'

The primary state would hold sole enforcement power over most rules, so the state where the buyer lives could not police the plan's terms and could only report compliance failures to the primary state.

The bill's own mandated study lists the risks its supporters would have to monitor: whether the change increases the number of uninsured and underinsured people, raises the cost of coverage for people with pre-existing conditions, and causes the elimination or reduction of benefits in policies sold in different states.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would create cheaper options for some buyers, mostly healthy ones, but the mechanism for doing so is stripping out the protections and required benefits of the buyer's own state, and it would hand enforcement to whichever state the insurer picks. The built-in safeguards — a disclosure notice, an appeals process, limits on health-status repricing — are narrow compared with the authority the bill takes away from the other 49 states. It is a structural shift in regulatory power toward insurers, and the open questions it leaves to a future study (effects on the uninsured, pre-existing-condition pricing, benefit elimination) are exactly the ones that matter most to people who get sick.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Biggs introduced the bill on January 4, 2021, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On February 2, 2021, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, and no further action was taken for the rest of the two-year Congress.

The bill would have let insurers choose a primary state whose laws govern coverage sold in all other states, exempting them from the other states' insurance laws except for a short list of protections.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained ground, because the bill never advanced: insurers did not get the authority to sell under a chosen state's lighter rules, and state-by-state insurance regulation and its consumer protections continued unchanged for the individual market.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State regulators and existing consumer rules

for.name: Rep. Andy Biggs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and offered no other members as cosponsors; it never advanced past referral.

against.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired took no action on the bill after referral; on February 2, 2021 it was sent to the Health Subcommittee, where no hearing or markup ever followed.

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican sponsor with zero cosponsors and no recorded votes, so the partisan split was never tested.

industries.note: Insurers could pick the state with rules they like best and sell plans in every other state exempt from those states' consumer protections, benefit mandates, and rate-change limits. Buyers would see cheaper plans, but often with skinnier coverage and enforcement left to the insurer's chosen state.

States would lose the power to regulate plans sold to their own residents, keeping only narrow tools: financial examinations, insolvency and guaranty-fund participation, fraud and unfair-claims rules, and the ability to seek court injunctions. The primary state would hold sole enforcement jurisdiction.
